segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we've seen how we can use the present to talk about the future in Spanish using voy a, vamos a, or using some future context: pronto (soon), mañana (tomorrow), la semana que viene (the week that comes, next week).

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But we can also use the present in Spanish to talk about the past, just as we can in English. In English and in Spanish, we have three ways to talk about the past, or three main ways to talk about the past. We can say, for example, "I ate", we can say "I was eating", and we can say "I have eaten".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now when we say "I have eaten", we're using "I have", which is the present, and then "eaten" is like a version of the verb which is kind of complicated in English. You say "I have eaten", "I have gone", "I have wanted". "Wanted", "eaten", "gone"—they're all very different. So that's kind of complicated in English, how to build that, but in Spanish, it's very simple.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we have "I ate", "I was eating", and "I have eaten". This "I have eaten" is going to be the first past that we learn, and we're actually using the present. Now this "have" is not tener. Tener we use for possession and we use with the combination of que to give this meaning of "have to".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now, the verb that we use for "have" in the sense of "I have eaten", "I have gone", in Spanish it's haber. Haber, h-a-b-e-r, and of course we have the silent h there in haber. Haber is "to have" in the sense of "I have eaten", but haber is extremely irregular. There is no habo. It's extremely irregular. But there is a very easy way we can remember all of the versions of haber, even though it's very irregular. What are the two vowel sounds that we have inside of the verb haber?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. We have a and e inside the word haber, and we're going to use that to help us remember the versions. Let's start with e. E all by itself means "I have". It's spelled h-e. And of course we have the silent h there from haber in he, h-e. "I have". We actually saw already one other verb that forms its "I" version in this way. What was "to know"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Sé. "I have" from haber is spelled h-e, just like sé from saber is spelled s-e. They're the only two verbs that form their "I" version in this way, in this very irregular way. So you get sé from saber and you get he from haber. Different from saber, all of the versions of haber are irregular. Now, "I" and "we" are connected. We can see how "we" is the plural of "I". "I" and then when I include you and I say "we", it's like the plural of "I". So "I" and "we" are connected. So, just knowing that, if you had to guess what is "we have", knowing that "I have" is he, what do you think you would guess?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This works with nouns and adjectives. So, it's a very good example of why, whilst we're avoiding grammatical terminology, we want to know what type of word we're dealing with, because different words behave in different ways. Nouns, words you can put "the" or "a" in front of—la semana, una semana, "the week", "a week"—and adjectives, words that describe, that you can put "is" in front of—"is red", "is tall"—these words use -s for plural, but we've never seen the verb do that, have we? What does the verb use for "we"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And what do they have in common, -amos, -emos, -imos?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Okay. So, if he is "I have", h-e, how do you think it might be "we have"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hemos. Good. So from haber, you get he and hemos. No? Now we don't want to memorize this. Like we said, we can think just this thought, just the thought, "What vowels do we have in haber? A and e. Oh, okay, e. E by itself is 'I', that's connected to 'we', he and hemos." Now we go to the other vowel: a, h-a. All by itself, h-a, ha means "she has", "it has", "he has", "you" (formal) "have". Now, I'm sure you can tell me the rest of them. What are the other versions? What is "they have"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So we start with this base of e and a, and we can remember that just by looking at the vowels that are inside haber, and then we can add on what we need. So we have he for "I have", hemos for "we have", we have ha, h-a, for "he", "she", "it", "you" formal have or has. You added an n, and what did you get?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And how would you say "you have", informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Has. Good. And that's your set: he, hemos, ha, has, han. So you have two key vowel sounds, e and a. He, hemos for "I" and for "we", for "I" and the plural of "I", which is "we", and then you have ha for "he", "she", "it", han for "they", has for "you" informal. Now we need to learn how to make "eaten", how to make "gone", how to make "wanted", if we want to say "I have eaten", "I have gone", "I have wanted". This is very simple in Spanish. -ar verbs will lose their -ar, they will lose their final -a-r, and they will put -ado on the end. So for example, we have "to speak", which is hablar. If you want to build "spoken", you take off that -ar and you put on -ado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablado. Now we can speak about the past. Now we can say "I have spoken". And we need to think about the two bits separately. "I have spoken".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. He hablado. "I haven't spoken". Where do you think the no is going to go? "I haven't spoken".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: In the beginning. No he hablado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Very good. No he hablado. "I haven't spoken". "We have spoken"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Perfect. Well done. Now, this is actually more useful, this past, than what you might think it is, because this is used even more in Spanish than it is in English. So, maybe you want the past "I spoke", but you can use for now "I have spoken". This "have" past is very popular and used much more than in English. So, how would you say "anticipation"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. How would you say "We have anticipated it"? So, there's a few things you have to think about. Think about them separately, then put them together. "We have anticipated it".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So to get "anticipated", you take away the -ar and you put -ado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And where does that lo go? Because anticipado is not like...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ah, it's changed now, so it's in the beginning. So, lo hemos anticipado.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo hemos anticipado. The word for "for", like in time—"We have anticipated it for a long time", for example—is por. Por.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You might know por favor, which means "please" in Spanish, which means "for a favor". Por favor, "for a favor". So this por is also "for" in the sense of for periods of time. So if you want to say "We have anticipated it for a long time", we will just say "We have anticipated it for much time". Maybe there's some bits in there you think you don't know, but we will see when we get to them. So the first bit is "We have anticipated it".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: "Time"? We saw briefly before that we have a word in English that we use for "time" that we only use with music. What was that word?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tempo. And how did it change in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Tiempo, yes. The e split. So, "We have anticipated it for a long time".

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Lo hemos anticipado por mucho tiempo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo hemos anticipado por mucho tiempo. Very good. Maybe you want to ask somebody, "Did you celebrate?" and you think "Oh, I don't know 'did' yet in Spanish". You can just say "Have you celebrated?" and that's fine. Like I said, it's used even more in Spanish than in English. So, some certain situations it might sound a little bit uncomfortable, the translation into English, but in Spanish most of the time it's going to be fine. So, "Have you celebrated?" Let's speak informally.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. What was the word for "where"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So, -ar verbs, we take away the -ar and we put -ado, and we get this version of the verb that we need after haber. Which in English has many different forms. Like I said, you have "gone", "wanted", "eaten"—changes a lot. But in Spanish, we get rid of the -ar and we put -ado. We said that "to take", and also sometimes "to drink", is tomar. Tomar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say "I have taken"?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "Has she taken it? Has she taken it?"

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: That's a guess. You're looking at me like it's a guess. I want you to establish your own thought process of how you're going to find it. So what's the first bit you need to think about? "Has she taken it?"

segments.text: Okay, so it's he and hemos for "I" and "we"...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ...so it's, oh, it's ha. It's just ha.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Ah. Sometimes I'm going to build you up step-by-step. Sometimes I'm just going to give you the sentence and you need to deconstruct what thoughts you need to have first, and to divide it up into various thoughts to get the sentence, resisting any temptation to guess or to say something that we're not sure of. You can be sure and be wrong, there's no problem there. Ah? But we want to think about it dividing the sentence up into each individual thing we need to think about. First: "she has" - ha. "She has taken" - ha tomado. "She has taken it" - it is lo. Where do I put the lo? Before the changed verb: lo ha tomado.
